title: Augustine's Hermeneutics of Love
author: Wyatt Graham
summary: Augustine's On Christian Teaching presents a hermeneutical theory grounded in the distinction between signs and things, use and enjoyment. Created things are changeable, temporary, corruptible—meant to be used, not enjoyed as final ends. Only God is unchanging and eternal, worthy of ultimate enjoyment. Purification of the heart comes through training oneself to see earthly goods as useful for drawing us toward God. Applied broadly, this framework teaches that reading, interpreting, and leadership are not mere intellectual exercises but transformative processes. The goal of understanding anything is not accumulation of facts but rightly ordered love—seeing everything as a theatre of God's glory and using all things for His sake.
points: Augustine's distinction between use and enjoyment reframes how leaders and learners engage with tools, knowledge, and people.
Created things—including data, feedback, relationships—are useful for drawing us toward higher ends, not ends in themselves.
Purification of the heart means training oneself to see through temporal, changeable things toward eternal truth.
Leadership and learning are transformative processes grounded in rightly ordered love, not mere information transfer.
quotes: Created things are good and useful, useful precisely because they draw us from changeable realities toward the one unchanging reality: God himself.

Our hearts are made to find ultimate pleasure in him. Augustine does not deny that we naturally take pleasure in food, friendship, and the goods of this life.” “Scripture exists to lead us to love. We will inevitably make mistakes, but we must not miss the central aim.” Archived from Wyatt Graham on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
